title: Noon
tomorrow: why did desert monks give the afternoon slump a demon's name?

cards: Phone alarms for meds, for water, for stretching. Some people set one for prayer too, and some people think that misses the point. The Church keeps both answers in the house.
At noon, by old custom, a church bell rings for the Angelus. And Paul, writing to the Thessalonians, says something that sounds like the opposite of a schedule: "Pray without ceasing."
So which is it: a slot, or the whole day?

teach.b: First, the Angelus. It retells one moment, the angel coming to Mary, in three short verses with a Hail Mary after each.
It opens: "The Angel of the Lord declared unto Mary," and the answer comes back, "And she conceived of the Holy Ghost."
Then Mary's own reply in Luke: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." Then John: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."

teach.h: THE CASE FOR A SET HOUR.
teach.b: Now the case for a set time, at its best. A psalm in the Douay says, "Evening and morning, and at noon I will speak and declare: and he shall hear my voice." Noon arrives whether you feel prayerful or not.
The bell doesn't wait for a mood, and that's the gift: the day can't run together.
Now the other case, at its best. Brother Lawrence, a Carmelite who worked in his monastery's kitchen, said the time of work was no different for him from the time of prayer.

In the noise of the kitchen, with people calling for different things at once, he held God as calmly as if he were kneeling before the Blessed Sacrament. Pray without ceasing means the whole day, not a slot.
Both are Catholic. The Church keeps fixed hours in its daily prayer, and it keeps Paul's line.
The noon pause sits between them: one minute fixed, so the rest of the day remembers.

how: Catholics pray the Angelus by custom in the morning, at noon and in the evening, often when a church bell rings; on Sundays the pope leads it at noon from a window over Saint Peter's Square.

games.q: the noon pause — tap the pairs.

s: the Angelus retells the angel's visit to Mary
its verses follow the annunciation in Luke and end with John's Word made flesh.
praying at set hours replaces praying the rest of the day
the Church keeps fixed hours and still keeps Paul's pray without ceasing.
Brother Lawrence felt close to God only in chapel
he said the busy kitchen was no different from the time of prayer.

games.q: two aunts argue at lunch. one sets a phone alarm to pray at noon; the other says scheduled prayer is fake. what does each have right?
o: the alarm keeps prayer from waiting on a mood; the other keeps it from shrinking to one slot.
the alarm aunt: prayer only really counts at fixed hours.
the other aunt: fixed times are a habit, not prayer.
games.why: the Church keeps both: the psalm's at noon I will speak, and Paul's pray without ceasing. each side's best case is real.

practice: Set down whatever is in your hands.
If you know the Angelus, say its three verses quietly aloud, a Hail Mary after each; if not, say only Mary's line, be it done to me according to thy word, and let the middle of the day stand still.

wordCard.voice: Noon. The middle of the day, where the Angelus sets one fixed minute.

orig.note: Latin, the prayer's first words, 'the angel of the Lord'; the Angelus is named for the first of them.

carryVoice: Your line: the noon pause. One fixed minute that reminds the rest of the day. Until tomorrow.
